title: Busy is not fast
lede: Everyone on the team is busy nine hours in ten, and everything is late. One hospital model, one real winter, and two desks fed the same hundred jobs show why: past about 85 % busy, the wait does not rise, it climbs.

commit.title: YOUR GUESS
commit.prompt: A team busy 9 hours of 10: how many job-lengths does a new job wait?

captions: Your team is busy 9 hours of every 10. Nobody idles.
Everyone fully used, so we are efficient. Right?
Busy 5 hours of 10: a new job waits about one job's length.
Busy 9 of 10: how many job-lengths? Pick a number.
1999, BMJ: a model of an English hospital's beds.
Above 85 of 100 beds full, the risk of no bed appears.
At 90 of 100: regular shortages, periodic crises.
Oct to Dec 2022, England's hospitals ran 92 of 100.
Same 100 arrivals, two desks. Each mark: one job ahead.
Half-busy desk: 100 arrivals found 99 jobs ahead.
Nine-tenths busy: the same 100 found 837 ahead.
837 ÷ 100 is 8.4 a job. The long run says 9.
Monday: which step runs above 85 % busy? What waits?
Limit: one desk, random work. Steadier work waits less.

brand.takeaway: Busy is not fast: at 90 %, a job waits nine.

sources: Bagust A, Place M, Posnett JW. Dynamics of bed use in accommodating emergency admissions: stochastic simulation model. BMJ 1999;319(7203):155–158. doi:10.1136/bmj.319.7203.155. Risks discernible above about 85 % average occupancy; regular bed shortages and periodic bed crises at 90 % or more.

NHS England. Bed Availability and Occupancy (KH03), Quarter 3 2023-24 Statistical Press Notice, February 2024: general and acute beds open overnight, average occupancy 92.0 % in Quarter 3 2022/23 (October–December 2022, revised).
Kleinrock L. Queueing Systems, Volume 1: Theory. Wiley, 1975. M/M/1: mean wait in queue = ρ/(1−ρ) × mean job length; an arrival finds on average ρ/(1−ρ) jobs in the system.
Kingman JFC. The single server queue in heavy traffic. Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 1961;57:902–904. Wait ≈ ρ/(1−ρ) × (cₐ² + cₛ²)/2 × job length.
Reinertsen DG. The Principles of Product Development Flow: Second Generation Lean Product Development. Celeritas, 2009. Ch. 3, Managing Queues: queue size against capacity utilisation.

This film's seeded simulation (claims.json formulas): one M/M/1 desk, mulberry32 seed 3, 2,000 warm-up jobs discarded, then 100 counted; the same random stream feeds both desks. Seed rule: the first seed from 1 whose two counts both land within 10 % of the long run (100 and 900).
This film's own construction: a day drawn as 10 hours, a ward drawn as 100 beds, the film-mode default guess.
honest: The count is one desk with random arrivals and random job sizes (M/M/1). Steadier work waits less: perfectly regular jobs at 90 % busy wait 4.5 job-lengths, half of 9 (Kingman). The curve keeps its shape.

The hospital case is a many-bed simulation (Bagust 1999) and a national average (NHS England); many parallel servers push the cliff later, they do not remove it. The film shows the cliff is real, not where a given ward's cliff sits.

The two desks are one seeded run of 100 arrivals each. Single runs at 90 % busy vary widely, from about 1 to 40 jobs ahead per arrival across seeds 1 to 60; seed 3 was chosen by a stated rule (the first seed whose two counts both land within 10 % of the long run).

tryit.title: Try it
tryit.note: Move how busy the desk is; the long-run wait follows ρ/(1−ρ).
